S: Subjective
Patient: Aloctan Caliope

DOB: 08/15/1970 (55 years old)

Chief Complaint: Progressive, painless arm weakness for 6 months.

History of Present Illness: The patient is a 55-year-old male who reports a 6-month history of progressive, painless weakness. The weakness began in his right arm and, over 3 months, spread to his left arm. It then progressed to involve the proximal arms and shoulder girdles symmetrically. He denies any associated sensory complaints or bladder involvement. Over the past 3 years, the weakness has worsened, particularly in the deltoid, biceps, elbow/wrist extensors, and intrinsic hand muscles. He now reports developing mild weakness in his neck and lower extremities over the past year. He denies any issues with breathing or swallowing.

O: Objective
Physical Examination:

General: Ambulatory, "man in the barrel" posture with arms hanging at the sides.

Motor: Significant atrophy of the shoulder girdles and upper extremities. Fasciculations noted over the upper extremities.

Upper Extremities:

Shoulder abduction/flexion/extension: 2/5 bilaterally (initial)

Elbow flexion: 2/5 bilaterally (initial)

Wrist/finger flexion: 4/5 (initial)

Wrist/finger extension: 3/5 (initial)

Finger abduction: 3/5 (initial)

Progression: By 3 years, strength in deltoid, biceps, elbow/wrist extensors, and hand intrinsic muscles was 0/5. Wrist and finger flexion was 3/5.

Lower Extremities: Normal strength (initial), progressed to 4/5 diffuse weakness by 6 years.

Facial/Bulbar/Respiratory: Normal throughout, except for neck flexion which progressed to 4/5 by 6 years.

Sensory: Normal to light touch, pinprick, and vibration throughout.

Reflexes: Absent in upper extremities. Normal in lower extremities.

Diagnostics:

Nerve Conduction Study (NCS):

Low amplitude median and ulnar compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs).

Normal median, ulnar, and radial sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs).

No evidence of conduction block or demyelination.

Electromyography (EMG): Active and chronic denervation changes with reduced recruitment in the upper extremities and cervical paraspinal muscles. Leg sparing noted initially.

Lab Tests:

Creatine Kinase (CK): Mildly elevated at 250 IU/L.

GM1 Ab titers: Normal.

Imaging: Brain and cervical spine MRI unremarkable.

Patient Name: Hymnius Nintaes
DOB: 04/15/1969
Date of Note: 08/22/2025

S (Subjective)
The patient is a 56-year-old previously healthy male presenting with a history of progressive, widespread muscle weakness and lower back pain. He reports a 1-year history of persistent lower back pain, which was initially managed with NSAIDs for 8 months without relief. Following this, he underwent a traditional medicinal procedure known as Ogosaraka in his native Kisii region of Kenya, which involved scarification of the lower back and insertion of a black metal powder into the incisions.

Approximately 4 months after this procedure, he developed progressive muscle weakness in his legs, arms, and neck, leading to a "head drop" and difficulty walking and carrying objects. He also reports difficulty with coughing and has experienced significant weight loss. The patient reports no improvement in his lower back pain since the procedure. He has since traveled to Norway to seek further medical care.

O (Objective)
Vitals: Not specified in the report.

Physical Exam:

General: Appears frail. Significant weight loss and generalized muscle atrophy noted.

Neurological:

Motor: Symmetrical, widespread muscle weakness in the legs, arms, and neck. Marked head drop. Difficulties with coughing observed.

Strength: Not formally graded but described as profoundly weak; patient can "hardly walk or carry heavy objects."

Back: Scarification marks noted along the lumbar region, consistent with the Ogosaraka procedure.

Labs/Imaging:

Bloodwork: Routine bloodwork reported as normal.

Liver Ultrasonography: Reported as normal despite slightly elevated liver enzymes.

MRI (lumbar): Herniated lumbar disc at L4/L5 and L5/S1.

Neurophysiological Exam (Neurography & EMG): Fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves found in several skeletal muscles, including the tongue (glossus muscle). The study concluded with evidence of widespread axonal damage and denervation.

Encounter Date: 08/22/2025

Chief Complaint: Follow-up for multiple indurated tumors and progressive joint stiffness.

S: Subjective
The patient is a 10-year-old female who was born with low birth weight (1700 g) and height (42 cm). She reportedly had normal development until age 6, when she presented with two palpable, firm tumors: a 3.5 cm mass in the right scapular region and a 5.5 cm mass at the dorsal vertebrae level. A biopsy at that time confirmed myofibromatosis. Since the initial diagnosis, her mother reports that the tumors have increased in size. The patient also experiences joint stiffness, particularly in her upper extremities, and has a limited range of motion in her neck, affecting rotation and flexion. The mother notes the patient has had short first toes with medial deviation since birth. The family history is notable for healthy non-consanguineous parents and two healthy siblings.

O: Objective
Physical Exam:

Vitals/Measurements: Weight at 10th percentile, height and head circumference at 50th percentile.

Musculoskeletal: Reduced neck mobility (flexion and rotation). Significant stiffness in shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints. Pronounced body asymmetry due to severe scoliosis. Multiple firm, indurated tumors are palpable in the scapular and infrascapular areas (biopsy sites) and a new tumor is noted in the right infra-axillary region.

Extremities: Short first toes with medial deviation.

Imaging:

Feet X-ray (Anteroposterior): Bilateral fusion of the proximal portion of the fourth and fifth metatarsals. Shortening of the first toe phalanges with medial deviation.
